prompts.text: Name a god or goddess of Norse mythology.
prompts.flavor: They already know how the world ends: with a wolf, a serpent and a great deal of fire.
prompts.rules: Any Norse god or goddess, Aesir or Vanir. Giants, monsters and beasts don't count, unless they were counted among the gods.

answers.lore: Gave an eye to drink from the well of wisdom, and hanged himself on the World Tree to learn the runes.
Thursday is named after him, as Wednesday is named after Odin.
A shape-shifter who fathered a wolf, a serpent and the queen of the dead, and gave birth to a horse.
So loved that everything swore never to harm him, except the mistletoe. Loki noticed.
Lost his hand in the jaws of the wolf Fenrir. Tuesday is named after him.
Watchman of the gods, who can hear grass grow. He will blow his horn when the world ends.
Queen of the dead who did not fall in battle. Half of her is flesh-coloured, half of her black.
Keeper of the apples that keep the gods young.
A god of archery and skiing. Almost nothing else about him survives.
A giantess who chose a husband by looking only at his feet. She picked the wrong pair.

prompts.text: Name a god or goddess of ancient Egypt.
prompts.flavor: They weighed the hearts of the dead against a feather. Something was always waiting for the heavy ones.
prompts.rules: Any god or goddess worshipped in ancient Egypt, by any of their names. Pharaohs don't count, whatever they thought.

answers.lore: Sailed across the sky by day and through the underworld by night, fighting the serpent Apep.
Jackal-headed god of embalming, who guided the dead to their judgement.
Murdered and cut into pieces by his brother, then pieced back together by Isis.
Herodotus says her festival at Bubastis drew 700,000 people, and more wine than the rest of the year.
A crocodile god. Sacred crocodiles in his temples wore earrings and bracelets.
The sun disc that Akhenaten tried to make Egypt's only god.
The sky, arched over the earth. She swallowed the sun every evening and gave birth to it every morning.
Goddess of truth and order. Her feather was weighed against the hearts of the dead.
A vast serpent of chaos who tried to swallow the sun every night.
Part lion, part hippo, part crocodile. She ate the hearts that weighed more than a feather.
A scarab-headed god who rolled the sun across the sky, as a dung beetle rolls its ball.
A bearded dwarf god who scared off demons, and so guarded homes and childbirth.
A pregnant hippo with a crocodile's back, who protected mothers and babies.
Djoser's architect, worshipped as a god of medicine two thousand years after his death.
A god invented under the Ptolemies, blending Osiris and the Apis bull with Greek gods.

prompts.text: Name a creature from myth or folklore.
prompts.flavor: Every map once had a margin where the monsters lived. Some of the margins are still there.
prompts.rules: Any monster or creature from the world's myths, legends and folklore, cryptids included. Creatures invented for books, films or games don't count.

answers.lore: Every five hundred years it burns itself on a pyre of spices and is reborn from the ashes.
Norwegian sailors said it was so vast that its back could be mistaken for an island.
The king of serpents, whose glance could kill. A weasel, a cock's crow or its own reflection could undo it.
An Irish spirit whose keening wail warns that someone in the family is about to die.
A figure of clay brought to life by Hebrew letters. In the Prague legend, erasing one letter undid it.
A spirit of winter and hunger from Algonquian lore, said to possess those who turn to eating people.
A whirlpool that swallowed the sea three times a day, and spat it out again.
A Japanese water imp with a dish of water in its head. Bow, and it bows back and spills its strength.
The horned companion of St Nicholas, who punishes naughty children in the Alps.
A horned jackrabbit, popularised by taxidermists in Wyoming in the 1930s.
A winged, red-eyed figure reported in Point Pleasant, West Virginia, in 1966 and 1967.
A huge black dog of East Anglia. In 1577 he is said to have burst into a church during a storm.
A Japanese fish with a human face. Eating its flesh grants a very long life.
A giant black spirit that rises from calm water and demands a ladle to swamp your boat. Give it one with no bottom.
A river hag who drags children under. Probably invented to keep them away from the water.
Storm-raising sea men of the Hebrides, who challenge captains to finish a rhyme.
A part-shark, part-octopus said to lurk in the blue holes of the Bahamas.
A giant catfish beneath Japan whose thrashing causes earthquakes.
The fiend who rules the evil spirits of the deep, in old sailors' lore. His locker is the sea floor.
An Orkney sea demon: a skinless horse and rider fused into one, with black blood in yellow veins.
A bird in Jewish legend so huge that its wings could blot out the sun.
An Alpine lizard-like worm with a cat's face, reported by mountain folk for centuries.
An Aztec water beast with a hand at the end of its tail, used to drag people under.
An Irish headless rider who carries his own head. When he stops, someone dies.
An Orkney sea serpent so huge that, when it died, its teeth became the Orkney, Shetland and Faroe islands.
A seven-headed sea serpent of Canaanite myth, an ancestor of the Bible's Leviathan.
Ghosts of the drowned who ask sailors for a ladle, to fill their boat and sink it.
A whale so vast that sailors land on it and light a fire, and are dragged under when it dives.
Pliny's heavy-headed beast of Ethiopia. Its head hangs low, which is lucky, because its gaze kills.
A creature of Arthurian legend with the noise of thirty couple of hounds in its belly, forever hunted.
A Swedish lake monster, protected by local law from 1986 until 2005.
The giant fish on which St Brendan's monks celebrated Easter, thinking it was an island.
A ghost whale of Japanese folklore: a skeleton that swims off the coast of Shimane, trailed by strange birds and fish.
A Norse sea monster so vast that sailors took it for islands. Whole shoals swam into its open mouth.
A shaggy, venomous dragon that survived Noah's flood, says the legend, and terrorised a French town.
A bull from medieval bestiaries whose horns curl uselessly backwards. It defends itself with burning dung.

prompts.text: Name a card of the tarot's Major Arcana.
prompts.flavor: Twenty-two cards to tell your fortune. The deck is not interested in what you would like to hear.
prompts.rules: Any of the 22 trump cards of a tarot deck. Names from older decks count too.

answers.lore: Number thirteen, and the card that frightens everyone. Readers insist it means change. They would.
Numbered zero, it wanders the whole deck. In French card games it survives as the Excuse.
Older decks show a street conjurer at a table, and call him the Juggler.
He hangs by one foot, calm, even serene. Old Italian decks called him the Traitor.
Struck by lightning, its crown blown off. Old decks call it the House of God.
Two dogs howl at the moon while a crayfish crawls out of the water.
Once called the Popess, perhaps after the legend of Pope Joan.
A sphinx on top, a serpent sliding down, and round it goes.
The last trumpet sounds and the dead rise from their graves.
An angel pours water from one cup into another, forever. Crowley's deck renamed it Art.
Called The Pope on older decks. The occultists of the Golden Dawn gave him a stranger name.

traps.reason: A Minor Arcana card. The Major Arcana are the 22 trumps.
Court cards belong to the Minor Arcana.
A playing card, a distant cousin of one of the trumps.
The whole deck. Which card?
